summary: A news feature dated September 12, 2023 on Hurricane Ida's September 4th strike on New Orleans and how it reopened debate over environmental policy. It covers storm damage, rising seas, levee performance after $14.5 billion in post-Katrina investment, the planned Green NOLA Initiative, economic costs, and community resilience. Voices differ on whether to prioritize immediate relief or long-term sustainability.
one_line: After Hurricane Ida hit New Orleans on September 4, officials, experts and residents debate levees, climate policy, recovery costs and community resilience.
key_facts: Hurricane Ida struck New Orleans on September 4th, and the article is dated September 12, 2023.
Ida tore roofs from homes, turned streets into rivers and knocked out power grids; early estimates project billions in repair and restoration costs.
Randall Dupre, a Lower Ninth Ward resident, said: "Our homes got stronger, our walls got higher - but water knows no boundaries."
Dr. Lila Dawson of Tulane University said Gulf of Mexico waters have consistently warmed, and "Warmer seas provide more moisture for storms to gather strength."
Dawson Hayes, a 78-year-old longtime resident, says every storm feels like "a roll of the dice."
Levee and flood wall investments totalling $14.5 billion since Katrina were stress tested by Ida and fared significantly better than expected, though cracks have appeared.
Engineer Sophia Torres, who has worked on the city's flood defenses since 2013, said "We learn from every storm but they keep changing."
Parts of Plaquemines Parish remain vulnerable even after upgrades.
Mayor Juliette LeBlanc said the city can no longer respond reactively and needs an inclusive strategy accounting for climate change.
The Green NOLA Initiative, due to be unveiled later in the month, aims to improve public transportation, add green spaces and incentivize renewable energy.
Clara Vargas argued that businesses are broken and people need immediate help, "not 10 years hence," rather than talk of going green.
The tourism industry was hard hit: hotels became makeshift shelters and many events were postponed or cancelled.
Economic analysts advocate an emergency disaster fund for both rebuilding and future-proofing; economist Elaine Rutherford stressed prevention over cure.
Community group "Rebuild NOLA" formed rapidly to distribute supplies and aid to the hardest-hit areas.
